1.title: The Word and the Run
1.context: Jonah son of Amittai is the prophet named in 2 Kings 14:25, who spoke of Israel's borders being restored under Jeroboam II. Nineveh was the great city of Assyria, the empire every small nation in the region feared, and Tarshish lay in the far west, as far as a ship from Joppa could carry a man.
1.question: God's assignment pointed Jonah toward his enemies and he bought a ticket the other way. Which direction is your own hardest assignment pointing?

1.title: The Storm and the Sleeping Prophet
1.context: Casting lots was a common way in the ancient world to identify guilt or a divine choice. The sailors each prayed to their own gods; the captain's rebuke is the chapter's irony, a pagan waking the prophet to pray. Jonah's confession names the LORD as maker of the sea he is fleeing across.
1.question: The crew saw the storm more clearly than the prophet did. Who in your life sees your situation honestly and has been trying to wake you?

1.title: Cast Me into the Sea
1.context: The sailors' reluctance is the text's own emphasis: they row harder to save the stranger before they will throw him in, and their prayer uses Israel's own concern, innocent blood. The great fish is appointed, the first of four appointments in the book; the word returns for the vine, the worm, and the wind.
1.question: The sailors feared shedding innocent blood for a man who had endangered them all. What does their care for a guilty stranger say to you?

1.title: The Prayer from Inside the Fish
1.context: Jonah's prayer is built from the Psalms' own phrases, the language of Israel's worship book carried into the deep. Its mood surprises many readers: it is thanksgiving, not a request for rescue, prayed before the deliverance is finished. Sheol is the realm of the dead in Hebrew thought.
1.question: Jonah thanked God from inside the fish, before anything had changed on the surface. What would thanksgiving before the answer look like in your situation?

1.title: Salvation Is from the LORD
1.context: The prayer's closing line is the book's thesis in five words. The fish's obedience is instant and unglamorous: commanded, it deposits the prophet on dry land, where the assignment he ran from is still waiting for him.
1.question: The deliverance changed Jonah's location but not yet his heart. Where has God rescued you without yet changing what you think about it?

2.title: The Word a Second Time
2.context: The second call repeats the first almost word for word; grace in this book sounds like an assignment restated, not revised. A three-day journey describes the city's breadth. Jonah's sermon as recorded is five words in Hebrew and carries no explicit call to repent and no named God, only a deadline.
2.question: God gave Jonah no softer message the second time, only the same one. What assignment in your life has come back unchanged?

2.title: The City Believes
2.context: Sackcloth and ashes were the region's public signs of grief and humiliation, and the fast's extension to the cattle shows a city performing repentance with everything it had. The king's Who knows echoes Israel's own prayers in disaster, the hope that God's character leaves a door open.
2.question: Nineveh repented on a deadline and a maybe. What have you been putting off that even a maybe should have been enough to start?

2.title: The Creed as a Complaint
2.context: Jonah's reason for running, withheld for three chapters, quotes Israel's creed from Exodus 34:6, gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion, as an accusation. His request to die echoes Elijah's prayer under the broom tree in 1 Kings 19, with the circumstances reversed: Elijah despaired after judgment fell; Jonah despairs because it did not.
2.question: Jonah knew God's character perfectly and it was the problem. Is there a trait of God you confess easily and resent in a particular case?

2.title: The Vine, the Worm, and the Wind
2.context: The vine is the same appointment word as the fish: God appoints the plant, the worm, and the east wind in sequence, a one-day sermon in objects. Jonah's pleasure in the plant is the only joy recorded of him in the book, and it is joy in his own comfort.
2.question: Jonah grieved a plant he never tended more than a city he was sent to. What small comfort of yours gets more of your heart than the people around it?

2.title: Should I Not Care?
2.context: The book ends without Jonah's answer, the only prophetic book to close on God's unanswered question. The 120,000 who cannot tell their right hand from their left pictures a population morally uninstructed, and the cattle, comic and tender at once, widen the mercy to the whole city as it actually is.
2.question: God's last word in the book is a question he leaves with the reader. What is your honest answer to it?
